title: Beyond Copilot: What AI tools are you *actually* finding useful in your gamedev workflow?
author: AuGKlasD
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I've been going down the AI gamedev rabbit hole for a few months now, and it feels like a lot of the discussion is either 'AI will replace all developers!' or 'It's just a fancy autocomplete.' I'm curious what tools people are \*actually\* integrating into their day-to-day workflow.

For me, it's been a few different categories:

\- \*\*Code Assistants (The Obvious One):\*\* GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT are great for boilerplate. I can ask for a basic inventory script or a state machine template and it saves a good chunk of time. But for core game logic or anything complex, I find I spend more time debugging its weird output than it would've taken to write it myself.

\- \*\*Asset Generation:\*\* Using Midjourney for concept art and character inspiration has been a game-changer for me as a solo dev who can't draw. It's great for getting the vibe right before committing to modeling. I've heard of people using it for textures too but haven't tried it much myself.

\- \*\*Full Game Creation Platforms:\*\* This is the area that feels the newest. I've been looking at tools that aim to remove the coding barrier entirely. For example, platforms like [MakeGamesWithAI](https://makegameswithai.com/) let you generate a playable game from a text prompt and then tweak it in an editor. It seems super interesting for rapid prototyping or for designers who want to test an idea without waiting on a programmer. It's a completely different approach from the code-first tools.

So, what's in your AI toolbox? Have you found any hidden gems for things like level design, sound generation, or QA testing? Or is it all still mostly hype for you?

comments.author: ichii3d
comments.body:
I mainly stick to Code in Rider using its integrated AI tools and access to all the major models. I mostly use Claudie and it's amazing. 

I have briefly explored 3D asset generation, if the model is something like a can, carrot, potato or whatever I would probably use it raw. But for everything else I would just use it to speed up block out. 

I explored AI assisted animation in Cascadur, but beyond basic exploration I didn't commit to a subscription yet.

When it comes to sound effects my exploration had me subscribing to existing libraries, so no AI there. But most sound websites also have AI tools for voice over or speech. The demos are impressive but again I have not reached the hurdle where I subscribe yet.

I'm still in early development so much of my stuff is being exploration, the production work I have been doing with AI is code.

replies.author: AuGKlasD
replies.body: What is Rider? I've never heard of that before. I've tried [Ludo.ai](http://Ludo.ai) for some asset generation and exporting and it actually worked pretty well. I also saw a post in here earlier about [https://www.autosprite.io/](https://www.autosprite.io/) \- I plan to try it tonight. It looks pretty neat, but you never know nowadays. I use SUNO to make background music and such for games, you should check it out if yo haven't. They don't do sound effects.

replies.author: AuGKlasD
replies.body: I see! I was a little confused because it kept saying jetbrains when i googled it - didn't realize they were the same thing. I use claude code + vs code - I guess it's something similar?

comments.author: CulturalFig1237
comments.body: I use Claude and Lovable for generating some projects like games. I find them easy to use.

comments.author: Synyster328
comments.body:
Codex CLI & Godot has been working well for me for general-purpose stuff on Windows.

I'm also building my own tooling for analyzing and modding games, while at the same time building out a custom voxel physics engine based on a fork of Godot.

replies.author: Light-Dream
replies.body:
Curious why you needed the custom voxel physics engine? 

I am also forking godot and built a complete curstom coding harness and agent deeply integrated with the engine, close to cursor experience but for games.

replies.author: Synyster328
replies.body: I wanted to use Godot for it's vibe coding ergonomics, and I started tinkering with voxel stuff... It wasn't so much that I wanted or needed the custom voxel physics engine, it was more of an inconsequential implementation side effect along the way as I iterated and pursued new ideas and got more excited about what I was able to achieve. I guess when you have automated intelligence at your fingertips the line that separates the foundation you're building on top of i.e., the engine, or byte code for modding compiled games at runtime, etc get blurred. You start to look at obstacles in a different way, like little quaint puzzles that would have been insurmountable without AI.

comments.author: biocidebynight
comments.body: Claude code CLI and Godot has been an awesome workflow for me

comments.author: injectmewitheuphoria
comments.body: Unity is my main engine, so I use Bezi to quickly get a mechanics and stuff set up and for anything that’s not scripting, and then Claude Code to refine the code. Used to use Cursor but Claude Code is just better from my experience.

replies.author: Light-Dream
replies.body: How much do u find bezi makes mistakes? How complex of a thing can u get it to work on? And how are the rate limits in different models?

replies.author: injectmewitheuphoria
replies.body: Pretty sure it runs on Claude (can’t select models in Bezi atm), so it makes mistakes on occasion but far less than ChatGPT back when I used that for game dev. If I use it as a guide, it’s been helping me build some prettt complex mechanics. It’s agentic capabilities are pretty good but I still need to push the limits
